title: A Rural Florida County Quietly Built a Flock Camera Network. Now It’s Dismantling It.
author: Alex DeLuca
content:
Just outside of Tallahassee, nestled among rolling hills and pecan groves of
Florida’s Big Bend region, Jefferson County is one of the most rural parts of
the state. With only 16,000 residents, it’s also the only county in Florida
with no traffic lights, a fact many locals will tell you with pride.

The farmers, retirees, and small business owners who call the county home have
long worked to preserve its distinct rural character. In 2020, residents
pressured Jefferson County commissioners to [pass a
resolution](https://ecbpublishing.com/commisioners-say-no-to-toll-road/)
opposing a proposed toll road, arguing it would invite national chains and
destroy the region’s pastoral landscape. Florida lawmakers later removed
Jefferson County as the planned terminus of the road. Last year, residents
again packed public meetings when a Love's Travel Stop was proposed. Despite
the revenue the project promised the county, the proposal was ultimately
[withdrawn](https://www.wtxl.com/news/local-news/in-your-
neighborhood/jefferson-county/jefferson-county-pastor-speaks-out-after-loves-
travel-stop-proposal-withdrawn-in-lloyd) after failing to gain enough support.

So it was a shock for Jefferson County residents to learn over the summer that
a sprawling network of automated surveillance cameras was quietly taking root
across the county.

“As far as I know, we weren’t notified. We didn't get to vote on it,” Kiley
Haselden, a 28-year-old farmer who grew up in Jefferson County, told _Bolts_.
“[The cameras] just showed up, and people started noticing.”

Records reviewed by _Bolts_ found that the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office
has been paying for Flock Safety’s automated license-plate readers (ALPRs)
since at least 2023, building an extensive network across the county.

[Deflock.org](http://deflock.org), a crowdsourced map of these cameras, has
flagged Jefferson County as home to 44 automated ALPRs—about 28 cameras per
10,000 residents—making it one of the densest license-plate-reader networks in
the country, according to the map. Most of the cameras listed on the map are
identified as Flock devices. Jefferson County Sheriff Mac McNeill had
previously touted the technology’s potential to help fight crime and improve
public safety.

But now, after years of expansion, growing opposition to the tech is causing
this network to be dismantled.

On Aug. 31, McNeill announced that Jefferson County would end its license-
plate-reader program and deactivate the cameras.

“After careful consideration and listening to the public’s feedback—including
both those who supported and those who opposed the use of this technology—I
have made the decision to discontinue the use of FLOCK/LPR camera technology
in Jefferson County,” McNeill wrote in a [Facebook
post](https://www.facebook.com/JeffersonSheriffFlorida/posts/pfbid02RSckHSV5vQrY8TmZC8hjRr9k1qMXTGy8h1XUwUAjuQgBHjqLZqHCjU99C3xm4ZbWl).

McNeill’s announcement came just hours after a
[decision](https://www.fox13news.com/news/flock-cameras-must-be-pulled-from-
florida-state-roads-within-30-days-desantis-orders) by Florida Governor Ron
DeSantis’ administration to remove Flock cameras from state roads. And it
added to other Florida law enforcement agencies that have decided to end their
ALPR programs, part of growing pushback in this and other red states against
Flock cameras, broadening the coalition [from civil rights advocates on the
left](https://boltsmag.org/verona-wisconsin-ends-contract-flock-ai-
surveillance-cameras/) who’d primarily pushed against this surveillance
network in recent years.

The [order](https://fdotwww.blob.core.windows.net/sitefinity/docs/default-
source/design/bulletins/eom26-01.pdf?sfvrsn=52938dee_1&Status=Master) by the
Florida Department of Transportation revoked existing permits for automated
license plate recognition systems, including Flock cameras, located within the
right-of-way of roads on the state highway system, citing “concerning reports
of misuse” and “data privacy concerns.” While the order does not amount to a
statewide ban on Flock cameras, it requires agencies to remove cameras located
in the state highway right-of-way.

McNeill, a Republican who was appointed sheriff by then-Governor Rick Scott in
2017 and then elected by voters in 2018, wrote that Jefferson County’s cameras
were “no longer operational” and were not collecting vehicle information,
though the full removal process could take months.

He defended the program as a way for a small, rural and fiscally constrained
office to stretch limited resources—a "force multiplier," in his words—and
said the technology had helped his deputies solve murders, locate missing and
endangered people, recover stolen vehicles and identify suspects. His office
did not provide specific cases to substantiate those claims.

“At the same time, technology is advancing at a pace that can be difficult for
our legal and judicial systems to keep up with,” McNeill wrote. “There will
always be a balance between giving law enforcement the tools necessary to
protect our communities and ensuring that those tools are used in a manner
that respects the constitutional rights and privacy of the citizens we serve.”

Since its founding in 2017, the Atlanta-based Flock Safety has rapidly
expanded its surveillance network, operating more than 120,000 automated
license plate readers across every state except Alaska. The devices use
artificial intelligence to capture license plates and other details about
vehicles, including their makes, models, and color. Information from
individual jurisdictions is compiled into a searchable database that
participating law enforcement agencies can use to access data collected by
cameras operated by other agencies, allowing police to track where vehicles
have been over time.

But the past year has seen a growing
[backlash](https://boltsmag.org/wisconsin-flock-and-revolving-door-of-
surveillance-companies/) against the technology, driven by privacy concerns
and reports of police [misusing](https://www.404media.co/cops-keep-getting-
arrested-for-using-flock-to-stalk-people/) the systems. Jurisdictions around
the country have ended their Flock contracts, and the opposition has crossed
party lines; DeSantis is the latest Republican state official to restrict
Flock operations, just days after Texas Governor Greg Abbott
[ordered](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/08/28/texas-greg-abbott-flock-
cameras-order-state-money/) all state agencies to pause funding for the
cameras in late August. The GOP governors raised concerns about government
surveillance and the collection of data on people who have not been accused of
crimes. Meanwhile [Angie Nixon](https://angienixon.com/priorities/),
Democrats’ U.S. Senate nominee in Florida, is warning that license-plate data
could be shared with federal immigration authorities and says she would work
to require warrants.

“This is kind of something that everybody agrees on,” Haselden told _Bolts_.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/485150905_1064723292357770_4086475708228188479_n.jpg)Jefferson
County, in the Big Bend region, is largely rural and sparsely populated, with
not even a single traffic light. (Facebook/Jefferson County Sheriff's Office -
Florida)

Jefferson County resident DaLila Gebhard, a 54-year-old whose family has lived
for generations in Wacissa, a tiny spring-fed river community in the county,
didn’t notice the cameras until several months ago. Now, she told _Bolts_ ,
she can’t drive more than a few miles without passing one—including the three
cameras located within a mile of her home.

She told _Bolts_ one of the cameras was recently knocked down and replaced
within weeks. The sheriff’s office did not respond to emails about the alleged
incident.

“I know most people feel the same way I do, that it’s invasive,” Gebhard told
_Bolts_. “We’re not criminals.”

She continued: “We are just a very tiny little village right here out in the
middle of nowhere. You know, everyone knows everybody. So it’s very odd that
we've got so much surveillance.”

Neither Gebhard nor Haselden recalls any county-led public forums to get
feedback on bringing the cameras into the county. In a Facebook
[group](https://www.facebook.com/groups/JC.SellTradeGive/) called Jefferson
County, FL Word of Mouth, residents recently debated the cameras. Some called
for their removal, while others expressed mixed feelings. One asked: “Why were
the residents not made aware before installation?”

Records reviewed by _Bolts_ show the sheriff’s office budgeted $25,000 for
Flock cameras in 2023-24, $42,947 in 2024-25 and $50,000 in 2025-26. The funds
represented less than one percent of the office’s overall budget each year,
but were growing; it proposed $55,000 for Flock and Arlo technology in
2026-27.

The office’s annual budgets, which included Flock cameras, went before
Jefferson County commissioners and were approved each time, but commission
meeting minutes reviewed by _Bolts_ show little evidence of any public
discussion about the surveillance technology.

McNeill did not respond to repeated interview requests and declined to answer
questions from _Bolts_ about why his office initially brought the cameras to
Jefferson County, what prompted his decision to end the program, and what will
happen to the sheriff’s office’s contract with Flock.

In an email to _Bolts_ , Marie Rigdon, an executive assistant at the sheriff’s
office, said McNeill is “not available for questions or comments regarding
this matter at this time.”

McNeill did explain some of his thinking at a public meeting on Sept. 3.
Acknowledging community pushback, he told the crowd, “We try to use technology
the best way we can. It just needs to be the right technology and the type of
technology the community supports.”

Flock leases its cameras and manages installation, maintenance, and removal,
according to its [website](https://www.flocksafety.com/press-center). If an
agency requests that cameras be turned off before removal, the company says it
can deactivate them remotely at any time.

When an agreement expires or is terminated, Flock says platform access is
disabled, cameras are remotely deactivated, and the company works with the
agency to “schedule physical removal.” A Flock Safety spokesperson did not
respond to questions from _Bolts_ about Jefferson County’s contract.

The physical removal of Flock cameras can take months even after an agency
ends its contract. In Verona, Wisconsin, the city ended its agreement with
Flock but found the cameras still installed months later. City officials said
Flock was slow to remove them, and the city eventually [covered the cameras
with plastic bags](https://boltsmag.org/verona-wisconsin-ends-contract-flock-
ai-surveillance-cameras/) until the company agreed to take them down.

During the Sept. 3 commission meeting, a Jefferson County resident rose to the
lectern to commend McNeill for getting rid of the Flock cameras.

“Normally I come here to complain, but today I’m happy,” the man said. He
praised DeSantis for removing the cameras from state roads and McNeill for
going “a step beyond that” by ending the sheriff’s office’s program on county
roads as well. “Amen, hallelujah,” he said.

He called the cameras “tremendously invasive,” saying the technology creates
“all sorts of bad things for innocent people like me that just ride on Highway
90 to go to church or go shopping.”

“Why do I need to be in that database?” he asked.

McNeill went to the lectern shortly afterward. He said the cameras had been a
“fantastic tool” for his office but that he ultimately had to weigh their
usefulness against residents’ concerns about privacy and constitutional
rights.

He said his office had been discussing what would happen to the Flock contract
when it expired, but DeSantis’ announcement accelerated the decision to end
the program.

“We want the community to feel comfortable in the type of policing we perform,
and we want them to be comfortable in the way that we serve them,” he said.

McNeill said he now hopes to redirect money that had been earmarked for the
cameras toward hiring another sheriff’s office deputy, something the resident
who spoke had previously written the sheriff to suggest.

“That’s where we should have our money going,” the man said. “Actual humans
solving actual crimes.”
